title: UK Plans to Curb Non-Compete Rules That Angered AI Startups
source_used: BBC News (own reporting) and Tech.eu; Bloomberg page blocked
key_facts: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a speech at a business summit in Manchester on 9 Oct 2026 that non-compete clauses in employment contracts had 'gone too far'.

Non-compete clauses restrict workers from joining rivals or starting competing firms after leaving a job; research cited by the government says around 5 million UK jobs are covered, typically for about six months.
He confirmed the government will press ahead with legislation so the clauses are 'no longer a barrier' to hiring, but did not set out the scope of the limits.
Details are expected alongside the Budget on 28 October, per the BBC.
The Recruitment and Employment Confederation warned against 'sweeping' changes, saying the clauses protect sensitive information and client relationships.
Tech.eu says the move follows a campaign by startups such as ElevenLabs and Synthesia; the first reports of the plan came from Politico and the Financial Times.
Tech.eu corrected an earlier version that said the government was banning the clauses.
quote_evidence: In a speech, the prime minister said the use of non-compete clauses in employment contracts had "gone too far" and was holding innovative UK companies back.
Burnham did not specify the scope of the restrictions he is planning, but suggested they would apply to the "everyday economy" as well as helping "promising start-ups and scaling firms".
The move follows a campaign by leading tech startups such as ElevenLabs and Synthesia to limit the use of non-compete clauses and extended notice periods.
why_it_matters_hint: A promise to change employment law could free workers to move and help startups hire, but the scope is still undecided.
notes: Bloomberg (403, robot check) was not readable; the BBC reports the speech directly and credits Politico and the Financial Times for the earlier report of the plan. A proposal, not yet law.
